power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Barriers to professional mental health help-seeking and considerations for school-based interventions among Secondary School adolescents: an exploratory qualitative study

author.affiliation:
The social sciences
								University of Ibadan
								
									Psychology
									Nigeria

text.text: Professional mental health service use remains low among adolescents, and school-based interventions are frequently designed without consulting the young people and clinicians they are intended to serve.

This exploratory qualitative study investigated the specific barriers to professional mental health help-seeking among Nigerian adolescents to inform the development of a culturally relevant school-based intervention.

Following the ethical principles of the Belmont Report, a focus group discussion was conducted with ten secondary school students (aged 13-16), alongside individual in-depth interviews with two students and key informant interviews with two practicing clinical psychologists in Ibadan, Nigeria.
Audio-recorded transcripts were verified and examined utilizing thematic analysis.
Eight core categories emerged from the data, highlighting a limited formal understanding of mental health among youth and a prominent gap between baseline knowledge and help-seeking behaviors.

While distress including depression, anxiety, addiction, and trauma was widely recognized through behavioral or academic declines, pervasive stigma and the fear of diagnostic labeling acted as dominant barriers to care, with nine out of ten adolescents refusing professional care pathways.
Friends served as primary confidants, while parental spiritual beliefs heavily gatekept formal psychological interventions.
Social media heavily informed adolescent self-image but introduced acute body-image concerns.
Notably, one student preferred using an artificial intelligence chatbot over human contact to ensure absolute confidentiality.

Participants requested foundational mental health literacy and coping skills delivered via brief, visual, interactive sessions, while clinicians anticipated systemic institutional implementation challenges regarding school leadership, funding deficits, and staffing constraints.
Interventions must target social stigma and privacy constraints directly alongside conceptual awareness.
Mental health conditions are common in adolescence.

The World Health Organization (2025) estimates that about one in seven young people aged 10 to 19 years experiences one, yet professional service use among adolescents is low in high-income and in low-and middleincome countries alike.
text.formatted: The World Health Organization <ref type="bibr">(2025)</ref> estimates that about one in seven young people aged 10 to 19 years experiences one, yet professional service use among adolescents is low in high-income and in low-and middleincome countries alike.

text.text: Professional help-seeking is a process rather than a single decision where a young person must recognise distress, decide it needs professional attention, know where to go, and overcome personal and social barriers to getting there.

Mental health literacy, defined by Jorm (2000) as the knowledge and beliefs that help people recognise, manage and prevent mental health problems, is often expected to drive help-seeking, but the evidence is mixed.
text.formatted: Mental health literacy, defined by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Jorm (2000)</ref> as the knowledge and beliefs that help people recognise, manage and prevent mental health problems, is often expected to drive help-seeking, but the evidence is mixed.

text.text: In an online survey of 300 UK university students, Gorczynski et al. (2020) found no significant correlation between mental health literacy and help-seeking, despite high levels of distress.
text.formatted: In an online survey of 300 UK university students, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Gorczynski et al. (2020)</ref> found no significant correlation between mental health literacy and help-seeking, despite high levels of distress.

text.text: In a meta-analysis of 62 studies of college students, Zhao et al. (2025) found a pooled prevalence of active help-seeking of 28%, against 41% for help-seeking intentions.
text.formatted: In a meta-analysis of 62 studies of college students, <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Zhao et al. (2025)</ref> found a pooled prevalence of active help-seeking of 28%, against 41% for help-seeking intentions.

text.text: Among 9,509 German school pupils, those with clinical depressive symptoms reported lower help-seeking intentions than those without (Baldofski et al., 2024), and among 2,434 adolescents in Bermuda fewer than half said they would seek help for a depression or social anxiety vignette, with stigma the most commonly endorsed barrier (Cavanagh et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Among 9,509 German school pupils, those with clinical depressive symptoms reported lower help-seeking intentions than those without <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Baldofski et al., 2024)</ref>, and among 2,434 adolescents in Bermuda fewer than half said they would seek help for a depression or social anxiety vignette, with stigma the most commonly endorsed barrier <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cavanagh et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A qualitative study of 32 young people with depressive symptoms similarly identified poor health literacy and attitudinal factors such as shame and wanting to handle the problem alone as obstacles to seeking treatment (Eigenhuis et al., 2021).
text.formatted: A qualitative study of 32 young people with depressive symptoms similarly identified poor health literacy and attitudinal factors such as shame and wanting to handle the problem alone as obstacles to seeking treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Eigenhuis et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Nigerian studies point in the same direction.

Low use of professional help and reliance on informal support have been reported among Nigerian students and young adults (Olayiwola-Adedoja et al., 2025; Orji et al., 2022; Isiogugu et al., 2026), and school-based programmes in southwest Nigeria have improved knowledge and attitudes towards mental illness (Dedeke et al., 2024; Ojumu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Low use of professional help and reliance on informal support have been reported among Nigerian students and young adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Olayiwola-Adedoja et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Orji et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Isiogugu et al., 2026)</ref>, and school-based programmes in southwest Nigeria have improved knowledge and attitudes towards mental illness <ref type="bibr">(Dedeke et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Ojumu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Little of this work, however, has asked adolescents and the clinicians who treat them, within the same study, why professional help is avoided and what a school programme should contain.
Young people may also be turning to new sources of support.

In a national survey of US adolescents and young adults aged 12 to 21 years, 19.2% had used AI chatbots for mental health advice in 2025, and 63.3% of those users had told no one (McBain et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In a national survey of US adolescents and young adults aged 12 to 21 years, 19.2% had used AI chatbots for mental health advice in 2025, and 63.3% of those users had told no one <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(McBain et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This study therefore explored the barriers to professional mental health help-seeking among Nigerian adolescents and gathered input from adolescents and clinical psychologists on how a school-based intervention could be designed.
An exploratory qualitative design was used to gather input for the development of a schoolbased intervention.
Three data sources were combined: a focus group discussion (FGD) and individual in-depth interviews (IDIs) with adolescents, and key informant interviews (KIIs) with clinical psychologists.
The analysis took a qualitative descriptive and pragmatic orientation, aiming to describe participants' perspectives and suggestions rather than to build theory.
Combining adolescents and clinicians allowed their accounts to be compared.
This study followed the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guidelines for reporting qualitative data (Tong et al., 2007).
text.formatted: This study followed the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guidelines for reporting qualitative data <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Tong et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The study was conducted in Ibadan, Oyo State, Nigeria.

Twelve people took part (Table 1): ten secondary school students, aged 13 to 16 years (median 15), from a private secondary school, and two clinical psychologists practising at the University College Hospital, Ibadan.
text.formatted: Twelve people took part (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>): ten secondary school students, aged 13 to 16 years (median 15), from a private secondary school, and two clinical psychologists practising at the University College Hospital, Ibadan.

text.text: Five of the students were female and five male; seven were in Senior Secondary School 2 (SS2) and three in SS1; nine were Christian and one was Muslim.
Two of the ten students also took part in IDIs.
The psychologists were one woman with three years' experience and one man with five years' experience, both holding an MSc in Clinical Psychology.
Participants were selected purposively for their relevance to adolescent mental health and help-seeking.
Adolescents were recruited through a purposive sampling approach at a selected private secondary school in Ibadan.
Initial contact was established via the school administration, who assisted in identifying eligible students.
To be included, adolescents had to be aged 13-19 years, currently enrolled in the school, and able to provide written parental consent alongside personal assent.
For the key informant interviews, clinical psychologists were purposively selected based on their active clinical practice with adolescent populations at the University College Hospital, Ibadan.
Transcripts were read repeatedly and analysed using thematic analysis following the six phases of Braun and Clarke (2006): familiarisation, coding, generating, reviewing, defining and naming themes.
text.formatted: Transcripts were read repeatedly and analysed using thematic analysis following the six phases of <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Braun and Clarke (2006)</ref>: familiarisation, coding, generating, reviewing, defining and naming themes.

text.text: Codes were grouped into categories that reflected the main issues raised, and categories were named for the finding they described.
Because many adolescent answers were brief, the number of participants giving an answer is reported where responses could be attributed, to show how widely a view was held and not to quantify it.
The transcripts were coded manually by the primary researcher.
To ensure the reliability and trustworthiness of the analysis, a second independent researcher reviewed the generated codes and the emerging thematic framework.
Discrepancies in coding were discussed and resolved through consensus.
Due to logistical constraints and school scheduling, transcript verification or member checking with the adolescent participants was not performed.
Quotations are verbatim, with spelling corrected and omissions marked by ellipses.
They are identified by data source and participant number (FGD-P1, IDI-P1) or by psychologist (KII-A, KII-B).
As a researcher grounded in the social sciences and psychology at the University of Ibadan, I acknowledge that my academic training shapes my interpretation of adolescent mental health.
Throughout data collection and analysis, I remained conscious of my position as an adult outsider, which could cause social desirability bias among the adolescents.

My prior assumption that stigma and low mental health literacy are the primary drivers of poor helpseeking was critically monitored to ensure that participants' alternative perspectives such as the role of school leadership barriers and digital tools were given equal weight in the thematic development.
Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the University of Ibadan/University College Hospital Ethical Review Committee (Ref: UI/EC/24/0098).
Written administrative permission was also secured from the principal of the participating school.

Prior to data collection, written informed consent was obtained from the clinical psychologists and the guardians (school principal) of the adolescents, while written assent was obtained directly from the minor participants.

To ensure participant safety, comprehensive contact information for accessible and confidential psychological support services at the University College Hospital was provided to all participants at the end of the sessions.
Participants were told that taking part was voluntary and that they could withdraw at any time, and transcripts were anonymised.

No body, I would rather speak to AI" [IDI-P1] and explained why: "It actually helped me a lot, I was able to find answers and all, and I could trust the AI tool because it wasn't going to tell others about what I am going through which prevented stigma" [IDI-P1] No other participant mentioned AI.
The reason given was confidentiality and the avoidance of stigma.
The same adolescent said they would not seek professional support (Category 3) and described withdrawing from other people (Category 2).

How to know when they are mentally wellbeing, how to cope with stress.

text.text: The second psychologist added staffing, structure and curriculum, and the risk that a programme's message would not be communicated clearly.

In this study, an exploratory qualitative inquiry with adolescents and clinical psychologists produced eight categories describing barriers to professional help-seeking and considerations for a school-based intervention.
The main finding was the gap between what adolescents knew and what they would do.
Most had little formal understanding of mental health, but nine of ten said nothing would encourage them to seek professional help, and stigma and fear of labelling were the reasons given.

This fits the international finding that literacy and help-seeking are only loosely linked (Gorczynski et al., 2020) and that intentions outrun action (Zhao et al., 2025), and it echoes qualitative work in which shame and wanting to cope alone, as well as limited health literacy, held young people back from treatment (Eigenhuis et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This fits the international finding that literacy and help-seeking are only loosely linked <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Gorczynski et al., 2020)</ref> and that intentions outrun action <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Zhao et al., 2025)</ref>, and it echoes qualitative work in which shame and wanting to cope alone, as well as limited health literacy, held young people back from treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Eigenhuis et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: It is also consistent with Nigerian reports of stigma and low use of professional help (Olayiwola-Adedoja et al., 2025; Orji et al., 2022).
text.formatted: It is also consistent with Nigerian reports of stigma and low use of professional help <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Olayiwola-Adedoja et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Orji et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The psychologists' disagreement about literacy is worth noting.
One saw adolescents as uninformed and uninterested, the other as informed but prone to mislabel themselves and to deny symptoms.

The adolescents' own answers showed limited conceptual knowledge, so the data do not settle the question, but they suggest that knowing what mental health is and recognising it in oneself are separate things, and that both may need teaching.
We offer this as an interpretation of a small dataset and not as a finding.

Friends, rather than parents or professionals, were the first source of support for most adolescents who named one, which is in line with reports that young people prefer people they know to formal services (McCabe et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Friends, rather than parents or professionals, were the first source of support for most adolescents who named one, which is in line with reports that young people prefer people they know to formal services <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(McCabe et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Peers could work in both directions: one adolescent would go to a professional if friends advised it, while the psychologists said friends who had attended therapy could encourage others to follow.
The adolescent who withdrew from everyone illustrates the limits of any approach that assumes a young person has a confidant.

Parents were described as the people who decide whether care is sought, and spiritual explanations of distress were said to delay it, an observation that comes from the psychologists and not from the adolescents.
Social media was described both as a source of information and as a source of risk.
The strongest adolescent account concerned body image, but it came from a single participant, so we treat it as an illustration rather than a pattern.

The psychologists' account of adolescents modelling what they see online, and of adolescents arriving after searching for their symptoms, points to social media as part of how mental health is learned and misread.
The AI finding came from one adolescent and should not be read as evidence that Nigerian adolescents generally prefer AI.
It is nevertheless worth reporting because the reason given, that the tool would not tell anyone, is the same reason that makes disclosure to people feel unsafe.

In a national US survey, 19.2% of adolescents and young adults had used AI chatbots for mental health advice and most users had told no one (McBain et al., 2026), and the authors noted that while chatbots may sidestep the stigma of disclosing to adults or peers, the privacy also carries risks if use is hidden from clinicians and trusted adults.
text.formatted: In a national US survey, 19.2% of adolescents and young adults had used AI chatbots for mental health advice and most users had told no one <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(McBain et al., 2026)</ref>, and the authors noted that while chatbots may sidestep the stigma of disclosing to adults or peers, the privacy also carries risks if use is hidden from clinicians and trusted adults.

text.text: Whether Nigerian adolescents use such tools, and what they believe about their confidentiality and limits, needs direct study.
Several considerations follow from these accounts, and each should be tested in further work.

First, content that only raises awareness is unlikely to be enough: stigma and fear of labelling were named by every group and would need to be addressed directly, alongside basic knowledge, symptom recognition and coping skills, which both groups asked for.
Second, delivery should be short, visual and interactive, as the psychologists advised, which agrees with a systematic review recommending interactive teaching with varied media (Lawal, 2025).
text.formatted: Second, delivery should be short, visual and interactive, as the psychologists advised, which agrees with a systematic review recommending interactive teaching with varied media <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Lawal, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Third, because friends were the main confidants, a peer element may be worth exploring.
Fourth, confidentiality needs explicit attention, both in how school-based support is described to students and in how a programme addresses digital sources of help.
Fifth, the psychologists expected the main implementation problems to be school leadership, funding, staffing and curriculum, so leadership support should be secured early.

A key strength of this study is that it gathered perspectives from both the adolescents and the clinical psychologists who treat them, with the primary patterns especially stigma and the fear of labelling appearing consistently across the FGD, IDIs, and KIIs.
Several limitations must be noted.
The sample size was small and restricted to one private school and one hospital in a single city, meaning the findings may not transfer to adolescents in public or rural settings.
Furthermore, many adolescent responses were brief, and several focus group questions only drew answers from a few participants, which limits the depth of the data.
Therefore, these findings should be understood as localized, stakeholder-informed considerations for intervention design rather than a generalizable account of all Nigerian adolescents or clinicians.

In this exploratory study, Nigerian adolescents had little formal knowledge of mental health and, in nine of ten cases, said nothing would encourage them to seek professional help, citing stigma and fear of labelling.
Friends were the first source of support, and one adolescent preferred an AI tool because it would not disclose what they shared.

Adolescents and psychologists agreed that a school programme should teach basic knowledge, symptom recognition and coping skills in short, interactive sessions, and the psychologists expected resistance from school leadership and funding constraints.

A school-based intervention in this setting is likely to need to address stigma and confidentiality as well as knowledge, and the considerations above should be tested in larger and more varied samples.

table.html: Data source n Participants Focus group discussion 10 Students aged 13-16 years; five female, five male; SS1 (FGD) (n = 3) and SS2 (n = 7); private school In-depth interviews (IDI) 2 Two of the FGD participants (FGD-P1 and FGD-P8), interviewed individually Key informant interviews 2 Clinical psychologists, University College Hospital, (KII) Ibadan (A: female, 3 years' experience; B: male, 5 years' experience) Data collection Three semi-structured guides were used. The KII guide had ten questions on the most prevalent adolescent problems, contributing factors, the influence of social media and technology, gaps in mental health literacy, misconceptions, factors that discourage and promote help-seeking, the content and delivery of a school programme, and implementation challenges in Nigeria. The FGD guide had ten questions on the meaning of mental health, problems common among young people, how stress is recognised, the effect of social media, sources of help, what makes professional help difficult, the influence of family, friends and beliefs, what would encourage professional help-seeking, and information needs. The IDI guide had six questions covering a personal experience of distress, coping and support, understanding of mental health and where it was learned, social media, how a decision to seek professional help would be made, and what students need most. All data collection sessions were conducted in English by the primary researcher in quiet, private rooms within the school and hospital premises to ensure confidentiality. The focus group discussion lasted approximately 60 minutes, while the individual in-depth interviews and key informant interviews ranged between 45 and 60 minutes. All sessions were audio-recorded with the explicit permission of the participants, and the recordings were subsequently transcribed verbatim for analysis.
